{{duplicate|[[2025 AMC 10B Problems/Problem 24|2025 AMC 10B #24]] and [[2025 AMC 12B Problems/Problem 20|2025 AMC 12B #20]]}} ==Problem 24== A frog hops along the number line according to the following rules. \qquad\bullet It starts at 0. \qquad\bullet If it is at 0, then it moves to 1 with probability \tfrac{1}{2} and it disappears with probability \tfrac{1}{2}. \qquad\bullet For n = 1, 2, or 3, if it is at n, then it moves to n+1 with probability \tfrac{1}{4}, it moves to n-1 with probability \tfrac{1}{4}, and it disappears with \qquad\phantom{\bullet} probability \tfrac{1}{2}. What is the probability that the frog reaches {4\,?} \textbf{(A) } \frac{1}{101} \qquad \textbf{(B) } \frac {1}{100} \qquad \textbf{(C) } \frac{1}{99} \qquad \textbf{(D) } \frac{1}{98} \qquad \textbf{(E) } \frac{1}{97} == Solution 1 (conditional probabilities of reaching 4) == We will solve this using the [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_total_probability law of total probability] (otherwise apparently known in Olympiad folklore as the method of "states", presumably reflecting the fact that these are kids who won't yet have studied formal/axiomatic probability theory). Firstly, we note that the probabilities of the frog taking each of its possible moves always depend only on its current position, and not on how it got there - in other words, the frog, just like coins or dice, 'has no memory'. Therefore, we can unambiguously define p_n as the probability of reaching 4 given that the frog is currently at position n. We want to find p_0 (since the frog starts at 0), and of course p_4 = 1. For each value of n, we now consider the conditional probabilities of reaching 4 given that the frog takes each of the possible moves from its current position. For instance, if the frog is at 3, it can go to 3-1 = 2 with probability \tfrac{1}{4}, and if it does, the conditional probability of it now reaching 4 from its new position at 2 is p_2 by definition; or it can go to 3+1 = 4, also with probability \tfrac{1}{4}, and if it does, the conditional probability is of course p_4 = 1; or it can disappear with probability \tfrac{1}{2}, and if it does, it can never reach 4, i.e. the conditional probability is 0. By analogous arguments at each of the other possible values of n, and then by applying the law of total probability, we deduce that \begin{align*}p_3 &= \frac{1}{4}p_4 + \frac{1}{4}p_2 \\ p_2 &= \frac{1}{4}p_3 + \frac{1}{4}p_1 \\ p_1 &= \frac{1}{4}p_2 + \frac{1}{4}p_0, \text{ and} \\ p_0 &= \frac{1}{2}p_1.\end{align*} Finally, by solving this system of equations, it follows that p_0 = \boxed{\textbf{(E) } \frac{1}{97}} (and incidentally, the probabilities for the frog's other possible starting positions are p_1 = \frac{2}{97}, p_2 = \frac{7}{97}, and p_3 = \frac{26}{97}). ~lprado == Solution 2 (conditional probabilities of taking single steps) == Let p_n be the probability that the frog eventually reaches position n, given that it is at position n-1. (This is well-defined because the frog 'has no memory', just as explained in Solution 1.) From position 0, the frog moves to 1 with probability \frac{1}{2}, or disappears with probability \frac{1}{2}. Hence p_1 = \frac{1}{2}. From position 1, the frog moves to 2 with probability \frac{1}{4}, back to 0 with probability \frac{1}{4}, or disappears with probability \frac{1}{2}. Thus, by the law of total probability (again similarly to in Solution 1) and using p_1 = \frac{1}{2} from above, we obtain p_2 = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{2} p_2 = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{8} p_2 \iff \frac{7}{8} p_2 = \frac{1}{4} \iff p_2 = \frac{2}{7}. We also now observe that if the frog is currently at 1 and wants to eventually reach 3, then it will necessarily have to pass through 2 first, since all of its possible moves only increase or decrease its position by 1. Accordingly, if the frog is at 2 and chooses to move back to 1, then the conditional probability that it eventually reaches 3 from its new position at 1 is equivalent to the probability that it eventually reaches 2 starting at 1 ''and then'' eventually reaches 3 starting at 2. That in turn reduces to the product of these two conditional probabilities: that of reaching 2 starting at 1 is p_2 = \frac{2}{7} from above, while that of reaching 3 starting at 2 is p_3. Using the law of total probability (analogously to above) at position 2, it follows that p_3 = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{2}{7} p_3 = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{14} p_3 \iff \frac{13}{14} p_3 = \frac{1}{4} \iff p_3 = \frac{7}{26}. Now from position 3, using p_3 = \frac{7}{26} as just found above, we deduce that p_4 = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{7}{26} p_4 \iff \frac{97}{104} p_4 = \frac{1}{4} \iff p_4 = \frac{26}{97}. Lastly, again because all of the frog's possible moves only increase or decrease its position by 1 (as explained above), the required probability that it eventually reaches 4 starting at 0 is equivalent to the probability that it eventually reaches 1 starting at 0, ''then'' reaches 2 starting at 1, ''then'' 3 starting at 2, ''and then'' 4 starting at 3. Similarly to above, this reduces to the product of the conditional probabilities p_1, p_2, p_3, and p_4, i.e. \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{2}{7} \cdot \frac{7}{26} \cdot \frac{26}{97} = \boxed{ \textbf{(E) } \frac{1}{97}}. ~MathKing555 == Solution 3 (recurrence relation) == As in Solution 1, let p_n be the probability of reaching 4 given that the frog is currently at position n, and observe that for n = 1,2,3, the frog can either go to position n+1 with probability \tfrac{1}{4}, in which case the conditional probability of it reaching 4 is precisely p_{n+1} by definition; or position n-1, also with probability \tfrac{1}{4}, giving a conditional probability of reaching 4 of p_{n-1}, again by definition; or else it disappears with probability \tfrac{1}{2}, in which case the conditional probability of reaching 4 is obviously 0. Therefore, by the law of total probability, we have the recurrence relation p_n = \frac{1}{4} \cdot p_{n+1} + \frac{1}{4} \cdot p_{n-1} + \frac{1}{2} \cdot 0 \iff 4p_n = p_{n+1}+p_{n-1} \iff p_{n+1}-4p_n+p_{n-1} = 0, \qquad \text{for } n = 1,2,3. Moreover, one boundary condition is obviously p_4 = 1, while the other concerns p_0: since the frog, starting at position 0, moves to 1 with probability \tfrac{1}{2}, in which case the conditional probability of it reaching 4 will be precisely p_1, or else disappears, also with probability \tfrac{1}{2}, the law of total probability again gives p_0 = \frac{1}{2} \cdot p_1 + \frac{1}{2} \cdot 0 \iff 2p_0 = p_1. We can now simply use standard methods to solve the above recurrence relation, subject to these two boundary conditions. Accordingly, the characteristic equation for this recurrence relation is \lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 1 = 0 \iff (\lambda-2)^2 = 2^2-1 \iff \lambda = 2 \pm \sqrt{3}, so its general solution is given by p_n = A\left(2+\sqrt{3}\right)^n + B\left(2-\sqrt{3}\right)^n for some constants A and B. Imposing the boundary conditions now yields 2p_0 = p_1 \iff 2(A \cdot 1 + B \cdot 1) = A\left(2+\sqrt{3}\right) + B\left(2-\sqrt{3}\right) \iff A\sqrt{3}-B\sqrt{3} = 0 \iff A = B, and hence p_4 = 1 \iff A\left(2+\sqrt{3}\right)^4+A\left(2-\sqrt{3}\right)^4 = 1 \iff A\left(97+56\sqrt{3}+97-56\sqrt{3}\right) = 1 \iff A = B = \frac{1}{194}. This means the particular solution is precisely p_n = \frac{1}{194}\left(2+\sqrt{3}\right)^n + \frac{1}{194}\left(2-\sqrt{3}\right)^n = \frac{1}{194}\left(\left(2+\sqrt{3}\right)^n+\left(2-\sqrt{3}\right)^n\right), and so, again as in Solution 1, the required probability is p_0 = \frac{1}{194}\cdot\left(1+1\right) = \boxed{ \textbf{(E) } \frac{1}{97}}.
